title: If an immutable class has a mutable field and the getter returns it directly, is the class still immutable, and how do you fix it (defensive copies for objects and collections)?
shortTitle: Immutable class with a mutable field returned directly — still immutable?

s1_definition.profdef: No, it is not truly immutable. If a class holds a reference to a mutable object, such as a `List`, a `Date`, or an array, and its getter returns that internal reference directly, then any caller can mutate the shared object through that reference, which changes the observable state of the supposedly immutable instance. The fix is defensive copying: copy the mutable object when it enters through the constructor and copy it again when it leaves through a getter, or return an unmodifiable view, so external code can never reach and modify the internal state.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, imagine a sealed account statement that is supposed to be final. But instead of giving Rajesh a photocopy, the clerk hands him the original master page that the bank keeps in its file. Rajesh can now scribble on that master page, and the bank's official record is changed, even though the statement was supposed to be unchangeable. That is exactly what returning the internal mutable reference does. The fix is for the clerk to always hand out a photocopy and keep the master locked away, which is defensive copying.
s1_definition.oneliner: Returning the internal mutable field directly breaks immutability, because callers can mutate shared state — fix it with defensive copies on both the constructor and the getter.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** No, it is not truly immutable. If a class holds a reference to a mutable object, such as a `List`, a `Date`, or an array, and its getter returns that internal reference directly, then any caller can mutate the shared object through that reference, which changes the observable state of the supposedly immutable instance. The fix is defensive copying: copy the mutable object when it enters through the constructor and copy it again when it leaves through a getter, or return an unmodifiable view, so external code can never reach and modify the internal state.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, imagine a sealed account statement that is supposed to be final. But instead of giving Rajesh a photocopy, the clerk hands him the original master page that the bank keeps in its file. Rajesh can now scribble on that master page, and the bank's official record is changed, even though the statement was supposed to be unchangeable. That is exactly what returning the internal mutable reference does. The fix is for the clerk to always hand out a photocopy and keep the master locked away, which is defensive copying.

**One line to remember:** Returning the internal mutable field directly breaks immutability, because callers can mutate shared state — fix it with defensive copies on both the constructor and the getter.

sections.s2_technical:
Immutability is about the observable state never changing after construction. Making fields private and final only prevents reassigning the reference; it does not prevent mutating the object the reference points to. A final `List` field cannot be pointed at a different list, but the list it points at can still have elements added or removed.

So if the getter returns the internal list reference directly, a caller can call add or remove on it, and the internal state changes. The field being final did not help, because the mutation happened on the object, not on the reference. The same applies to a `Date`, which has mutating setters, and to arrays, which are always mutable.

There is a second leak point: the constructor. If the constructor simply stores the caller's reference, the caller still holds their own reference to the same object and can mutate it after construction. So the object is compromised from the moment it is built.

The fix is defensive copying at both boundaries. In the constructor, copy the incoming mutable object into a fresh internal object, so the internal state is independent of the caller's reference. In the getter, return a copy or an unmodifiable view, so the caller cannot reach the internal object. For collections, `new ArrayList<>(source)` is a copy, and `Collections.unmodifiableList` or `List.copyOf` gives an immutable view. For a `Date`, you copy with `new Date(date.getTime())`, though modern code uses the immutable `java.time` types that need no copying. For arrays, you use `clone` or `Arrays.copyOf`.

A senior nuance is that a shallow copy is sometimes not enough. If the list contains mutable elements, copying the list still shares the elements, so callers could mutate those. For true deep immutability you either store immutable element types or make deep copies. In banking, the safest design is to use immutable building blocks throughout, such as `BigDecimal` and immutable value types, so that most defensive copying is only needed at collection and array boundaries. Another nuance is that `List.copyOf` both copies and makes the result unmodifiable, which is often the cleanest single-step fix.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank built a Statement class it believed was immutable, with private final fields. But a bug let a caller add fake entries to the statement after it was issued, corrupting the audit trail. This is exactly the leak from returning the internal mutable list directly.

Problem 2 — Investigation showed two leaks: the constructor stored the caller's list, and the getter returned the internal list. This is exactly the two-boundary problem.

Problem 3 — The fix is defensive copies in and out. The demo shows the broken version being tampered with, then the fixed version blocking the tamper. This is exactly the before-and-after fix.

The code has a broken `LeakyStatement`, a fixed `SafeStatement`, and an `ImmutableLeakDemo` main class contrasting them.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a statement for SAV2001 with one genuine entry, then attempts to inject fake entries.

Step 1: The broken LeakyStatement is created, storing the caller's list reference directly. The caller still holds a reference to the exact same list.

Step 2: The caller adds a fake entry to its own list. Because LeakyStatement shares that list, the statement now shows the fake entry. This is the constructor leak.

Step 3: The caller then calls the getter and adds another fake entry to the returned list. Because the getter returned the internal reference, this also corrupts the statement. This is the getter leak. The leaky statement is now corrupted with two fake entries.

Step 4: The fixed SafeStatement is created. In its constructor it copies the incoming list into a fresh ArrayList, so the internal list is independent of the caller's.

Step 5: The caller adds a fake entry to its original list. Because SafeStatement copied the list, its internal state is unaffected. The constructor leak is closed.

Step 6: The caller calls the getter and tries to add a fake entry. Because the getter returns an unmodifiable view, the add throws UnsupportedOperationException, which is caught and logged. The getter leak is closed, and the safe statement remains intact with only the genuine entry.

```text
SEVERE: LEAKY statement corrupted: [SAV2001 debit 50000, FAKE via constructor leak, FAKE via getter leak]
INFO: SAFE statement: getter tamper blocked
INFO: SAFE statement intact: [SAV2001 debit 50000]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  ─── BROKEN (LeakyStatement) ───
  callerList ──┐
               ├──► stored directly (LEAK 1)
  internal ────┘  (same object!)
     │ getEntries() returns same ref (LEAK 2)
     ▼
  caller mutates → statement CORRUPTED

  ─── FIXED (SafeStatement) ───
  callerList ──► new ArrayList<>(callerList)  ← copy IN (independent)
                      │
                      ▼ internal list (isolated)
  getEntries() ──► Collections.unmodifiableList(internal)  ← safe OUT
     │ caller.add() → UnsupportedOperationException ✓
     ▼
  statement INTACT
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Closing Both Leak Points ═══

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐   ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │  <<final>> LeakyStatement     │   │  <<final>> SafeStatement      │
  │  - final entries: List        │   │  - final entries: List        │
  │  ctor: this.entries = in  ✗   │   │  ctor: = new ArrayList<>(in) ✓│
  │  getEntries(): return entries ✗│   │  getEntries(): unmodifiable ✓ │
  └───────────────────────────────┘   └───────────────────────────────┘

  Defensive-copy cheat sheet:
   List  → new ArrayList<>(src) / List.copyOf(src) / unmodifiableList
   Set   → new HashSet<>(src) / Set.copyOf(src)
   Map   → new HashMap<>(src) / Map.copyOf(src)
   Date  → new Date(d.getTime())  (better: use java.time immutable)
   array → src.clone() / Arrays.copyOf(src, len)

  Deep vs shallow:
   shallow copy shares ELEMENTS; if elements are mutable, deep-copy
   or store immutable element types for true deep immutability.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
No, if an immutable class has a mutable field and its getter returns that field directly, the class is not truly immutable. The reason is that making a field private and final only prevents reassigning the reference; it does nothing to stop someone mutating the object the reference points to. A final list field cannot be pointed at a different list, but the list itself can still have elements added or removed. So if the getter hands out the internal list reference, any caller can mutate it, and the observable state of the supposedly immutable object changes.

There are actually two leak points, and both must be closed. The first is the constructor: if it simply stores the caller's reference, the caller keeps their own reference and can mutate the object after construction, so it is compromised from birth. The second is the getter: if it returns the internal reference, callers can mutate through it.

The fix is defensive copying at both boundaries. In the constructor I copy the incoming mutable object into a fresh internal object, so my state is independent of the caller. In the getter I return a copy or an unmodifiable view, so the caller can never reach my internal object. For a list I use a new ArrayList or List dot copyOf, for a set or map the equivalent copy, for an old-style Date I copy with its time value though I prefer the immutable java dot time types, and for an array I clone it.

One senior subtlety I always add is that a shallow copy may not be enough. If the collection holds mutable elements, copying the collection still shares those elements, so for true deep immutability I either store immutable element types or make deep copies. In our banking code the safest design is to use immutable building blocks everywhere, like BigDecimal and immutable value types, so defensive copying is only needed at collection and array boundaries. This exact bug bit us once, where a supposedly final statement got fake entries injected both through the constructor and through the getter, corrupting the audit trail. After adding defensive copies in and out, the statement became genuinely tamper-proof, which is non-negotiable for a banking audit record.
